name: Lena Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head grower at Hollow Lane, a cooperative farm, so the eleven of us who work it also own it. It's about ninety hectares: field vegetables for our box scheme, oats, a few hundred laying hens and a pig unit at the bottom by the stream. My day starts with the hens at six, then I'm with the field team planning who's on harvest and who's on weeding, and by evening I'm packing boxes or fixing the irrigation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the planning: getting the leeks and the pigs and the rotation to line up so nothing's wasted. What wears me out is that we all own it and none of us earn much from it. My partner Sami drives buses, we've a mortgage on a small house in the village, and most months we're down to nothing by the twentieth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I tell people now: it's a useful tool for some jobs. I use it now and then to rough out a planting plan or tidy up the box newsletter. Online I'd probably say the real story is still who owns the land and who sets the prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means not much changes for me, and that's fine. The things that hurt us are the supermarket prices and the weather, not software. I'd go on feeling stretched, but stretched in a way I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are. At the spring members' meeting I'd suggest we try one AI tool for the box orders, because Hana loses two evenings a week on the spreadsheet. Otherwise I'd keep my head down and get the leeks in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit tired. It's the life I already know, money worries and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money actually go each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage first, then Noor's school trip fund, then the van insurance. Sami's overtime is what saves us. If he gets his hours cut, we're borrowing from my brother by the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss if AI did a bit of your paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, honestly. I'd happily hand over the egg sales records. I didn't do a degree in agriculture to type up egg sales.

S0.say: It's a useful tool for some jobs; I use it now and then for planting plans and the box newsletter. The real story is still who owns the land and who sets the prices.
S0.think: Not much changes for me, and that's fine. What hurts us is supermarket prices and the weather, not software, so I'd stay stretched, but in a way I know.
S0.do: Carries on running the field team and suggests at the spring members' meeting that the cooperative tries one AI tool for box orders. Otherwise keeps her head down and keeps the season on track.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit tired, since it's the life she already knows, money worries included.
S0.quote: I'd happily hand over the egg sales records. I didn't do a degree in agriculture to type up egg sales.
S0.fieldNote: Lena talks like a planner, always thinking in rotations and members' meetings. The hype picture barely registers as a threat; her worries are prices and her partner's overtime. She's comfortable using AI for small office jobs and sees no loss in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the machines should belong to the people doing the work, and that's exactly why a cooperative makes sense. I'd say we need public money to help small farms share kit, not just big estates buying it. That's my line online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about the weeding robots. Half of our field work is hand weeding, and a robot that can tell a carrot from a thistle would make two of our members' jobs pointless. And we'd be the ones voting on it, which is a horrible position to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a farm near us had tried one for a full season, then I'd go and look at it with my own eyes. If it works, I'd push for the co-op to share one with the Brookside farm rather than borrow alone. I'd also start putting the egg money in a separate pot so we've a bit of cushion before any change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that members' vote actually be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. Hana and Marco do most of the weeding and they're friends. I'd want us to agree first that nobody leaves, and that they move onto the box scheme or the pigs instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it took the hand weeding off us, I'd welcome it for my back. I'm forty-three and I can feel every bed of onions. I just want the savings to stay with us, not go to whoever rents us the robot.

S1.say: The machines should belong to the people doing the work, which is exactly why a cooperative makes sense. Small farms need public money to share kit, not just big estates buying it.
S1.think: I'd worry about the weeding robots, because half our field work is hand weeding. A robot that can tell a carrot from a thistle makes two of our members' jobs pointless, and we'd be the ones voting on it.
S1.do: Waits until a nearby farm has run a weeding robot for a full season and goes to see it in person. If it works, pushes for the cooperative to share one with a neighbouring farm, and starts putting egg money into a separate cushion.
S1.feel: Uneasy rather than frightened, lying awake doing sums.
S1.quote: Half of our field work is hand weeding, and a robot that can tell a carrot from a thistle would make two of our members' jobs pointless.
S1.fieldNote: Being a part-owner makes this picture personal in an unusual way: she might have to vote to make friends' work pointless. She's typically cautious, wanting to see a full season on someone else's farm first. She'd welcome the robot for her own back if the savings stayed with the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what happens when nobody regulates anything, and I'd be angry about it in public. I'd be calling for the government to step in for food workers before the shelves go empty. I'd say small farms like ours can't compete with an estate running robots day and night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think Hollow Lane would struggle to last two years against that. If big farms are growing veg with robots, our box prices look silly overnight. And Sami's buses would be first in line for driverless ones, so it's both our wages at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call an emergency members' meeting the first week. We'd cut our own wages before cutting anyone, and I'd apply for every rural support grant going. At home we'd stop everything that isn't food, heat and the mortgage, and I'd ask the bank about switching to interest-only for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it. I'd be up at three o'clock most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor and Idris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Mum and Dad are both working it out and they're not to worry about school. Noor's thirteen and she'd see through that, so I'd tell her more. Idris is ten, he'd want to know if the hens are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd usually wait for proof before changing. Does that still work with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's what scares me. My whole way is to watch others first. With two years there's nobody to watch, everyone's finding out at once.

S2.say: This is what happens when nobody regulates anything. The government has to step in for food workers, because a small farm like ours can't compete with an estate running robots day and night.
S2.think: I don't think Hollow Lane lasts two years against that, because our box prices would look silly overnight. And Sami's buses would go driverless early, so it's both our wages at once.
S2.do: Calls an emergency members' meeting in the first week and proposes wage cuts across the cooperative before any job cuts. Applies for every rural support grant, cuts household spending to food, heat and mortgage, and asks the bank about a year of interest-only payments.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with her stomach dropping and nights awake at three in the morning.
S2.quote: My whole way is to watch others first. With two years there's nobody to watch, everyone's finding out at once.
S2.fieldNote: The speed takes away her usual method of waiting for proof, and she names that herself. The double hit, her cooperative and her partner's bus job, is what lifts this to real alarm. She still thinks first of the group, cutting everyone's wages before anyone's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them. I'd push our farmers' network to ask for a public fund to help small farms buy shared robots, and for retraining money for people who lose work. I'd be writing that to the council and anyone else who'd read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for us to change but not enough for me to feel safe. I'd be forty-eight, the kids would be in their late teens, and I'd still have the mortgage. I'd probably still have a job, but on less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd go on the short course at the agricultural college on running field robots, once a few others from the network had done it and said it was worth it. I'd move the co-op toward things a robot doesn't do well: the box scheme, farm days, selling direct. And we'd keep feeding that egg-money pot, even twenty pounds a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be tired, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does three extra years change for you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns a panic into a plan. With two years I'm cutting wages. With five, I can learn the kit, change what we sell, and maybe keep everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools more yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I'd seen them work. I'd use them for the rotation and the box orders. I'd still want my own eyes on the fields every morning.

S3.say: We've got five years, so let's use them. Small farms need a public fund for shared robots and retraining money for anyone who loses work.
S3.think: Five years is enough for us to change but not enough for me to feel safe. I'd be 48 with the mortgage and teenagers, probably still working but on less money.
S3.do: Takes a short college course on running field robots once others in her network recommend it. Moves the cooperative toward direct selling and farm days, uses AI for rotations and orders, and keeps adding to the egg-money cushion.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, tired yet feeling she's steering.
S3.quote: It turns a panic into a plan. With two years I'm cutting wages. With five, I can learn the kit, change what we sell, and maybe keep everyone.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years make the biggest difference for her, because they let her follow her normal pattern of waiting for proof and then moving. She'd retrain, but only after peers had tried it. She still sees herself as keeping the group together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, and if it isn't fair that's a choice somebody made. I'd keep pushing for public ownership of the big kit, or at least shared ownership for farmers. I'd want food workers at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be all right, more or less. By 2036 Noor and Idris would be grown, and I'd have had years to change the farm. The fear's still there, but it's in the back seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course in the first couple of years, after seeing how it went for others. I'd help the co-op join with two or three farms to buy shared kit, and I'd move us toward more selling direct and teaching. And I'd want Noor to study something she loves, not something safe, because nobody knows what safe is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. Like a long forecast with rain somewhere in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would any of the members end up leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one or two would choose to. Marco's always wanted to run his own place. I'd want it to be their choice, not the robot's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could change one thing now to get ready for this, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get some savings, honestly. Everything else I can plan. Having nothing in the bank means every choice is made with a knife at your back.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, and if it isn't fair that's somebody's choice. Farmers should share ownership of the big kit and food workers should be at the table.
S4.think: Privately I think we'd be more or less all right. The kids would be grown and I'd have had years to change the farm, so the fear's there but in the back seat.
S4.do: Takes the robotics course in the first couple of years after seeing others' results. Helps the cooperative club together with two or three farms to buy shared kit, moves into direct sales and teaching, and encourages her daughter to study what she loves.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly settled, like a long forecast with rain somewhere in it.
S4.quote: Having nothing in the bank means every choice is made with a knife at your back.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's close to calm, and the remaining worry is about money, not skills. Her line about savings sums up her whole situation: she can plan well but has no buffer. She keeps returning to fairness and shared ownership, consistent with her politics.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is government money to keep small farms and their workers going while it shakes out, and a fund for co-ops and small farms to share the machines instead of losing to estates that can buy them outright.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. If robots make farming cheap, people with money will buy up more land. I'd want somebody watching who owns the fields in ten years, because that's where it really ends up.

headlineQuote: If robots make farming cheap, people with money will buy up more land.
portrait: Lena Farah is a 43-year-old head grower and part-owner at a small workers' cooperative farm with vegetables, oats, hens and pigs, married to a bus driver, with two children, a mortgage and almost no savings. She's a careful planner who uses AI now and then for paperwork and likes to see new kit proven on someone else's farm before trying it. She's calm in the hype picture, uneasy about weeding robots in the steady one, and alarmed by a two-year AGI arrival that would hit both her farm and her partner's job. With five or ten years she turns fear into a plan: learning the kit, sharing machines with neighbours and keeping every member in work.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no one to watch and learn from first, and both her cooperative and her partner's bus job would be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: Government money to keep small farms and their workers going through the change, and a fund for cooperatives and small farms to share robots.
